summary: Describes the Simple Two-way Active Measurement Protocol (STAMP), which measures one-way and round-trip performance metrics such as delay, delay variation and packet loss by sending test packets between two endpoints.

plainLanguage.summary: STAMP sends test packets between two endpoints and returns timing information for measuring network performance. The returned sequence numbers can also help identify whether packets were lost on the way out, on the way back, or across the full trip.

questions: how to measure delay and packet loss with twamp-light
what udp port does stamp use
subtitle: A two-way test protocol for measuring delay, variation, and packet loss.

tldr.problem: Operators needed a clearly specified and interoperable way to run active network tests without requiring the test protocol itself to define session management and control.
tldr.mechanism: A Session-Sender sends numbered UDP test packets with timestamps to a Session-Reflector, which returns packets containing receive and transmit times. The reflector can operate with or without per-session test state.
tldr.outcome: STAMP measures one-way and round-trip delay, delay variation, and packet loss. Its unauthenticated mode is designed to interwork with TWAMP Light, and the unit metadata says it is updated by RFC 8972.

today: RFC 8762 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 8972. It specifies STAMP test packets and reflector behavior.

sections.title: Why STAMP Was Specified
sections.content:
STAMP is an active test protocol for measuring delay, delay variation, and packet loss in one-way and round-trip traffic. Earlier experience with TWAMP and TWAMP Light showed that implementations could be difficult to make interoperable when test behavior was not specified clearly enough.

STAMP defines the test packet exchange. Configuration and management of senders, reflectors, and sessions remain outside this RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: STAMP gives two endpoints a defined way to exchange network test packets. Operators can use the returned timing and sequence information to measure a path.

sections.title: Sender and Reflector Behavior
sections.content:
A STAMP session is a bidirectional packet flow between one Session-Sender and one Session-Reflector. The sender sends test packets over UDP, using port 862 as the default destination port. The reflector returns a packet of the same size by default.

A stateless reflector keeps no test state and copies the incoming sequence number, so the sender can calculate round-trip loss. A stateful reflector keeps per-session state and uses its own sequence number, allowing the sender to distinguish forward from backward loss.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender sends a UDP test packet, and the reflector sends a reply with timing information. A stateful reflector counts its own replies, which helps locate packet loss by direction.

sections.title: The Sender Test Packet
sections.content:
The unauthenticated base sender packet is 44 octets; the authenticated form is 112 octets. The packet includes a sequence number, a timestamp, an error estimate, and fields marked Must Be Zero (MBZ). The sequence number starts at zero for each session and increases by one for each packet.

Nodes MUST support the NTP version 4 64-bit timestamp format and MAY support the truncated PTPv2 format. In authenticated mode, the packet includes a 16-octet HMAC and has enough padding to make its size a multiple of 16 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: Each sender packet carries a sequence number and timestamp. The authenticated form also carries a message authentication code so the receiver can check that the packet was not changed.

sections.title: The Reflector Reply
sections.content:
The reflector checks the base test packet and returns a packet of matching size. Its reply includes the reflector's sequence number and timestamps for receipt and transmission, along with copies of the sender's sequence number, timestamp, and error estimate.

The reply also carries the sender's IP TTL or IPv6 Hop Limit from the received packet. Extra data beyond the base packet is copied so packet sizes remain symmetrical.
sections.plainLanguage: The reply records when the reflector received and sent the test packet. It also copies the sender's timing and sequence fields so the sender can compare both ends.

sections.title: Integrity and Confidentiality
sections.content:
Authenticated mode uses HMAC-SHA-256 truncated to 128 bits. The 16-octet HMAC covers the first six blocks, or 96 octets, and MUST be checked as early as possible. Key management and key distribution are outside the scope of this RFC.

STAMP does not encrypt test packets. A session that needs confidentiality MUST use a secured transport, such as an IPsec tunnel or Datagram Transport Layer Security.
sections.plainLanguage: The authenticated mode can detect changes to a test packet, but it does not hide the packet's contents. Use a secured transport when confidentiality is needed.

sections.title: Interworking with TWAMP Light
sections.content:
STAMP is designed to interwork with TWAMP Light in unauthenticated mode. The protocols use different HMAC algorithms in authenticated mode, so that mode is not treated as interoperable.

A STAMP sender may use a port other than 862 when communicating with a TWAMP Light reflector that does not support the default port. A STAMP reflector also handles packets smaller or larger than its base packet by returning a base reply or copying the extra content.
sections.plainLanguage: STAMP can exchange unauthenticated test packets with TWAMP Light. Their authenticated packet formats differ, so authenticated interworking is not specified.

sections.title: Operational and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC intends STAMP for production networks, including measurement against service-level agreements. Operators MUST estimate test traffic load and analyze its effect on existing services. Use over the Internet must be agreed by users of the sender and reflector hosts before a session starts.

Control and management of a test session MUST use secured transport. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: Test traffic uses network capacity, so operators need to assess its effects and obtain agreement before running a session. Session control and management must use secured transport.
